offence_severity: 302 (punishment for murder) - minimum 7 years, maximum death or life imprisonment
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the dying declaration of the deceased, which was recorded in accordance with established practice and procedure, and found it to be a truthful version of the events leading to her death.
witness_credibility: The court assessed that the hostile witnesses supported the prosecution case to some extent, and their hostility was a relevant consideration but not the sole determinative factor for the accused's guilt.

legal_representation.accused: Ram Naresh Yadav, Dr. Kailash Chand
legal_representation.state: Kamal Mohan Gupta, Mohd. Zahid Hussain, Sanjeev Kumar

investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the dying declaration of the deceased, recorded in accordance with established practice and procedures, is a truthful version of the events leading to her death and can form the sole basis of conviction if it is true, reliable, and recorded properly.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the hostility of the witnesses undermines the reliability of the dying declaration and that the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond a reasonable doubt due to the lack of corroboration from key witnesses.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that a dying declaration can form the sole basis of conviction if it is true, reliable, and recorded in accordance with established practice and principles, and that the hostility of witnesses is a relevant consideration but not the sole determinative factor.
precedent_relied_upon: Khusha/ Rao v. State of Bombay AIR 1958 SC 22; State of Uttar Pradesh v. Ram Sagar Yadav and Ors. (1985) 1 SCC 552; Munnu Raja and Anr. v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1976) 3 SCC 104; Bhajju @ Karan Singh v. State of Madhya Pradesh (2012) 4 SCC 327; Mrinal Das v. State of Tripura (2011) 9 SCC 479
